text.p: The mark ended the day slightly firmer on its European cross rates as the Bundesbank held key interest rates unchanged despite a weaker-than expected German employment report for November.

Adjusted pan-German unemployment rose a further 50,000 during the month, higher than the 30,000 rise expected by market economists, and pushed the seasonally-adjusted jobless rate up to 10.7 percent from 10.6 percent in October.
The German labour ministry said it expected total unemployment to remain above the four-million level for another few months at least.

"The German labour report was weak but I think the markets had already got even more bearish on the German economy than it currently warrants, especially in relation to interest rate expectations," said Michael Burke, economist at Citibank.
The Bundesbank central council later left its key interest rates unchanged at its fortnightly meeting.

The Bundesbank said it was exempting short-term repurchase agreements from its minimum reserve requirements. However, analysts said there was no monetary policy effect likely or intended from the move which was aimed at bringing Germany in line with other European countries ahead of monetary union.
At 1600 GMT, the mark was trading at 3.3800/05 French francs compared with 3.3771/76 late Wednesday. Mark/lira was at 987.40/45 compared with 982.50/983.00.

The focus of the day's trading was on sterling's fresh lunge lower, as profit-taking was exaggerated by Bank of England governor Eddie George's benign interest rate comments, and by the yen's continued recovery amid Japanese rate rise concerns.

The latter in particular tends to disproportionately hit high yielding European convergence plays funded in cheap yen. A rise in the Swiss franc, also increasingly used as funding unit for convergence plays, had a similar effect, traders said.

The dollar's retreat in late trading also helped underpin the mark, although there was no single reason for its pullback. Some cited pressure from a technical correction in the U.S. bond market ahead of tomorrow's November U.S. employment report while others cited rumours of European central bank gold sales.
The gold price has been hit severely in recent sessions to three-year lows as talk of European central bank reserve adjustments ahead of EMU have circulated.
There is a concern these central banks, who some say will have excess of gold and dollar currency reserves after EMU, are looking to off-load these to help bridge fiscal deficits.
Elsewhere, the Swedish crown was hit by an unexpected half- point cut in both the Riksbank's lending and deposit rates to 5.25 percent and 3.75 percent respectively.
Analysts said that together with improving nominal inflation rates and inflation expectations, the Riksbank may now lower its key repo rate further.

The lira was unnerved, meantime, as Prime Minister Romano Prodi called for a lower cost of money. The Bank of Italy remains stubborn in keeping short rates high despite a drop in inflation to 2.6 percent in November from 3.0 in October.
